blocks.text: Follow the alleles across generationsMendel studied traits in pea plants and used controlled crosses between lines with contrasting forms. In a simple example, let R represent round seeds and r wrinkled seeds, with complete dominance of R. A true-breeding RR line crossed with rr produces Rr offspring in the F1 generation.Every F1 individual can have the round phenotype while still carrying the r allele. blocks.text: Segregation explains reappearanceAn Rr individual forms gametes containing R or r. The alleles segregate as homologous chromosomes separate during meiosis. In the simple model, each allele has a one-half chance of entering a gamete.When two Rr individuals produce the F2 generation, gametes can combine as RR, Rr, rR or rr. Rr and rR name the same heterozygous genotype. The expected genotype ratio is 1 RR : 2 Rr : 1 rr. With complete dominance, the expected phenotype ratio is 3 round : 1 wrinkled.The wrinkled phenotype reappears because an offspring can receive r from both parents. No new r mutation is required to explain that result.

exactOwnedParagraphs.text: An Rr individual forms gametes containing R or r. The alleles segregate as homologous chromosomes separate during meiosis. In the simple model, each allele has a one-half chance of entering a gamete.

When two Rr individuals produce the F2 generation, gametes can combine as RR, Rr, rR or rr. Rr and rR name the same heterozygous genotype. The expected genotype ratio is 1 RR : 2 Rr : 1 rr. With complete dominance, the expected phenotype ratio is 3 round : 1 wrinkled.

blocks.text: Choose a tester with a known contributionAn individual with a dominant phenotype may be AA or Aa. Crossing it with aa creates a useful test because the recessive tester can contribute only a. The phenotype of the offspring then provides evidence about the unknown parent's contribution.If the unknown parent is AA, every offspring is expected to be Aa and show the dominant phenotype. If the unknown parent is Aa, the expected offspring are half Aa and half aa. A recessive offspring therefore demonstrates that the unknown parent contributed a, under the stated simple model.

blocks.text: A flower colour disappears, then returns Mendel crossed pea plants from lines with purple flowers and lines with white flowers. The first offspring generation had purple flowers. The colours had not produced the pale-purple blend that a blending explanation would suggest. When that generation reproduced, white flowers appeared again. How could a phenotype disappear for a generation without its allele being lost? Keep the distinction from lesson01 in view. A phenotype is an expressed characteristic, such as flower colour. A genotype is the allele combination at the locus being considered. An allele is a version of a gene, and a locus is the gene's position on a chromosome. An allele can be present in the genotype even when its associated recessive phenotype is not expressed. Know what was crossed A true-breeding line consistently produces the same form of the relevant trait when bred within the line under the stated conditions. That description comes from breeding history, not from looking at one plant. In the simple one-gene model used here, the contrasting true-breeding lines are homozygous: each individual has two copies of the same allele at that locus. Controlled crossing makes the parentage known. A pea flower can supply pollen and can also contain eggs. Pollination transfers pollen to the receiving flower; a sperm cell delivered through the pollen tube can later join an egg. That joining is fertilisation. To compare chosen lines, Mendel controlled which plant supplied the pollen instead of allowing an unintended pollen donor or self-pollination to change the cross. The chosen starting parents form the P generation. Their offspring form the F1 generation, the first filial generation. Offspring produced when the F1 plants reproduce in the specified design form the F2 generation. These labels tell you how the generations are related. They do not mean that every P individual is homozygous or every F1 individual is heterozygous in every possible experiment. Follow the same question using seed shape We will now move from flower colour to another pea characteristic: round or wrinkled seeds. Use R for the round-seed allele and r for the wrinkled-seed allele. Under complete dominance, RR and Rr seeds are round; rr seeds are wrinkled. Rr is a heterozygote because its two alleles differ. Dominant describes this heterozygote's phenotype; it does not mean common, better or more likely to be inherited. In this model, the shape being scored belongs to each offspring seed with its own genotype. A seed can then be grown into a plant, which will contribute alleles to the next generation of seeds. Keep those generations separate: a parent's genotype helps determine its gametes, while the genotype of a particular offspring seed comes from the two gametes that formed it.

blocks.text: Each parent contributes one allele A chromosome is a DNA-bearing structure carrying many genes. In an ordinary diploid cell there are two chromosome sets. The corresponding chromosomes form a homologous pair: one came from each parent, and both carry the same kinds of genes at corresponding loci. An Rr individual has R at the seed-shape locus on one homologue and r at that locus on the other. Before meiosis, DNA is copied. Each chromosome then consists of two sister chromatids, the copied versions joined together. Copying an R-bearing chromosome produces two R-bearing sister copies; it does not turn r into R or mix the two allele versions. We are following ordinary copying and separation, without a mutation changing the allele. Meiosis reduces the chromosome sets from two to one. The homologous chromosomes separate in the first division. The sister chromatids separate in the second division, with no further DNA copying between those divisions. A cell with one chromosome set is haploid. In a flowering plant, the reproductive life cycle produces haploid gametes after this reduction. We only need to follow the allele contribution here: an egg or sperm carries one allele at this locus, not the parent's whole pair. Thus an RR parent can contribute R; an rr parent can contribute r; and an Rr parent can contribute R or r. A probability is the chance of an outcome under the stated conditions. Under ordinary segregation, either allele from the heterozygote has a probability of one half of being in a gamete. Dominance does not decide which chromosome separates into that gamete. The two allele versions remain distinct as they are passed on.

blocks.text: Worked example From the starting cross to the second generation Start with the true-breeding seed-shape lines: RR × rr. The multiplication-style cross sign means these are the two parents being crossed; it is not an instruction to multiply the letters. The RR parent contributes R in its gametes. The rr parent contributes r. At fertilisation, one egg and one sperm join, restoring a pair of alleles in the zygote, the first cell of the offspring. Every combination available in this cross is therefore Rr. Applying the phenotype rule after combining the alleles gives round F1 seeds. The r allele is still present in each seed's genotype. Grow the F1 seeds into plants. When an Rr F1 plant self-pollinates, its eggs can carry R or r and its sperm can carry R or r. The same allele-combination reasoning applies to a controlled cross between two Rr F1 plants. The F2 cross is Rr × Rr. Read the small grid from its edges inward. The left edge gives an egg's allele; the top edge gives a sperm's allele. Each interior entry combines those two contributions. The edges represent gamete possibilities, and the interior entries represent offspring genotypes. They are not the same kind of cell. Possible F2 allele combinations from Rr × Rr Egg allele ↓ / sperm allele →R, probability ½r, probability ½ R, probability ½RR — roundRr — round r, probability ½rR — roundrr — wrinkled Follow the lower-right entry first. The egg contributes r and the sperm contributes r, so the offspring is rr and expresses the wrinkled phenotype. Neither allele had to be recreated. Both were available in the F1 parents before they formed gametes. Now compare the upper-right and lower-left entries. Rr and rR are the same heterozygous genotype; the written order only shows which gamete supplied which allele in this table. The gene in this model is autosomal, meaning it is on a chromosome other than a sex chromosome. Here the complete-dominance rule is the same whichever parent supplied R. With equal R/r gamete probabilities and random fertilisation, the four contribution pairs are equally likely. They group into 1 RR : 2 Rr : 1 rr for genotype. RR and Rr both express round seeds, so the phenotype grouping is 3 round : 1 wrinkled. Grouping by appearance combines two genotype categories; it does not change the allele pairs inside them. This distinction separates two processes. Segregation produces single-allele contributions as homologous chromosomes separate during gamete production. Random fertilisation combines one parent's gamete with the other's. Chromosomes aligning in one parent's meiosis do not themselves join that parent's gamete to a gamete from another parent. Repair the two process labels The allele contributions below are possible, but a student's process labels are reversed. The arrows summarize allele movement; they omit DNA copying and the intermediate cells. A predicted ratio is not an offspring schedule The 3:1 phenotype ratio predicts three quarters round and one quarter wrinkled over many offspring from this cross. It does not assign a compulsory order to the offspring or guarantee those exact proportions in a small group. Each fertilisation is another event; an earlier round seed does not make a later seed owe the cross a wrinkled result. Mendel's reported seed-shape counts included 5,474 round and 1,850 wrinkled seeds, approximately 2.96 round for each wrinkled seed. That is close to 3:1, not exactly 3:1. The useful evidence is a repeated pattern that the inheritance model explains, not a perfect match from every small sample. For this prediction, we have used known parental genotypes, ordinary equal segregation, random fertilisation and the stated complete-dominance relationship. We also assume that the phenotypes are expressed reliably and recorded without one kind of offspring being selectively lost from the count. Chance can change the observed proportions among possible outcomes. A consistent mismatch can also mean that a starting genotype, observation or model assumption needs checking. Mendel inferred that inherited factors remained distinct from the breeding patterns he observed. The later chromosome account explains how those factors can be copied, separated and combined. The law of segregation explains the allele contributions; complete dominance explains why the Rr heterozygote looks round in this model. Neither rule says that the r allele was destroyed. Does reversing the parents reverse the result? Use the same ordinary autosomal seed-shape model: RR and Rr offspring seeds are round; rr offspring seeds are wrinkled. The allele has the same effect whether it arrives in the egg or in the sperm. The genotypes below are known from the breeding lines. Follow one egg contribution and one sperm contribution in each cross, give the resulting genotype and phenotype, and use those contributions to evaluate the grower's claim. In cross B, the RR egg parent supplies R and the rr pollen parent supplies r. The offspring are again Rr and round. Reversing which parent supplied the alleles does not change the pair or its phenotype under the stated model.The grower's claim omits the sperm's genetic contribution and assigns the receiving plant's phenotype directly to the offspring. Fertilisation combines contributions from both parents. The conclusion concerns this specified autosomal seed-shape model; it is not a rule that every biological characteristic is unaffected by parental origin or growing conditions.Check your response: show the egg and sperm allele in both crosses; distinguish the offspring seed from the plant carrying it; apply the same complete-dominance rule to the resulting genotype; explain why the receiving plant's appearance alone does not determine the answer. The returning phenotype now has a continuous explanation: alleles persist through copying, separate into contributions, and can meet again at fertilisation. Lesson03 will make the grid and probability operations systematic. Lesson05 will ask whether following one gene's alleles tells us anything about a second gene. For now, keep the contribution mechanism and the phenotype rule separate.

Place those gametes on the edges and combine one from each parent in each cell.The resulting possibilities are Aa and aa in equal proportions. With complete dominance, half are expected to have the dominant phenotype and half the recessive phenotype. The square shows why the 1:1 ratio applies; a 3:1 ratio would be the wrong shortcut for this cross.A single-trait cross: Aa × AaView largerEach row and column represents a gamete. Four equally likely combinations give a 1:2:1 genotype ratio under the stated model. A is completely dominant to a. Schematic — not to scale.

exactOwnedParagraphs.text: A Punnett square organizes combinations of gametes. For Aa × aa, the first parent produces A or a gametes; the second produces only a. Place those gametes on the edges and combine one from each parent in each cell.

The resulting possibilities are Aa and aa in equal proportions. With complete dominance, half are expected to have the dominant phenotype and half the recessive phenotype. The square shows why the 1:1 ratio applies; a 3:1 ratio would be the wrong shortcut for this cross.

blocks.text: Count the outcome that was actually asked forFor Aa × Aa, the four equally likely combinations are AA, Aa, aA and aa. Grouping the two heterozygous combinations gives probabilities of 1/4 AA, 1/2 Aa and 1/4 aa. The dominant phenotype has probability 3/4 under complete dominance.Genotype probability and phenotype probability therefore can differ. “Heterozygous” refers to two of the four combinations, while “dominant phenotype” includes three. Mark the requested group before choosing your numerator.When converting to an expected number, multiply by the total. If 80 offspring each have a 1/4 chance of aa, the expected number is 80 × 0.25 = 20. The result is an expectation, not a promise.

exactOwnedParagraphs.text: For Aa × Aa, the four equally likely combinations are AA, Aa, aA and aa. Grouping the two heterozygous combinations gives probabilities of 1/4 AA, 1/2 Aa and 1/4 aa. The dominant phenotype has probability 3/4 under complete dominance.

Genotype probability and phenotype probability therefore can differ. “Heterozygous” refers to two of the four combinations, while “dominant phenotype” includes three. Mark the requested group before choosing your numerator.
When converting to an expected number, multiply by the total. If 80 offspring each have a 1/4 chance of aa, the expected number is 80 × 0.25 = 20. The result is an expectation, not a promise.

blocks.text: Worked examplePredict a phenotype and an expected countIn a stated complete-dominance model, Tt is crossed with tt. Predict the fraction and expected number of recessive offspring among 60.Tt produces T and t gametes; tt produces t gametes.The equally likely combinations are Tt and tt.The recessive phenotype is tt, probability 1/2.Expected number = 60 × 1/2 = 30.Check: the other expected 30 have the dominant phenotype; observed counts can vary.

Independent offspring do not compensate for earlier outcomesIn the simple model, one offspring's genotype does not force the next offspring to be different. If two Aa parents have several dominant-phenotype offspring, the modeled probability for the next offspring is still 1/4 recessive.For specified independent events, multiply probabilities. Two recessive offspring in a row from Aa × Aa have probability 1/4 × 1/4 = 1/16. Do not confuse this ordered event with “at least one recessive among two,” which asks for a different set of outcomes.State assumptions such as complete dominance and ordinary segregation. They determine which genotype combinations count toward a phenotype.

blocks.text: Choose a tester with a known contributionAn individual with a dominant phenotype may be AA or Aa. Crossing it with aa creates a useful test because the recessive tester can contribute only a. The phenotype of the offspring then provides evidence about the unknown parent's contribution.If the unknown parent is AA, every offspring is expected to be Aa and show the dominant phenotype. If the unknown parent is Aa, the expected offspring are half Aa and half aa. A recessive offspring therefore demonstrates that the unknown parent contributed a, under the stated simple model.

exactOwnedParagraphs.text: An individual with a dominant phenotype may be AA or Aa. Crossing it with aa creates a useful test because the recessive tester can contribute only a. The phenotype of the offspring then provides evidence about the unknown parent's contribution.

If the unknown parent is AA, every offspring is expected to be Aa and show the dominant phenotype. If the unknown parent is Aa, the expected offspring are half Aa and half aa. A recessive offspring therefore demonstrates that the unknown parent contributed a, under the stated simple model.

blocks.text: Positive evidence and absence of evidence differOne aa offspring from B_ × bb means the dominant-phenotype parent must carry the recessive allele, assuming the model, parentage and observations are correct. It is heterozygous.By contrast, several dominant offspring do not logically prove the parent is homozygous. An Aa parent can, by chance, produce a run of A-bearing gametes. For four independent offspring in an Aa × aa cross, the probability that all show the dominant phenotype is (1/2)⁴ = 1/16.More offspring with no recessive phenotype generally strengthen the homozygous interpretation, but finite samples still require cautious wording. Say what the evidence supports and what remains possible.

exactOwnedParagraphs.text: One aa offspring from B_ × bb means the dominant-phenotype parent must carry the recessive allele, assuming the model, parentage and observations are correct. It is heterozygous.

By contrast, several dominant offspring do not logically prove the parent is homozygous. An Aa parent can, by chance, produce a run of A-bearing gametes. For four independent offspring in an Aa × aa cross, the probability that all show the dominant phenotype is (1/2)⁴ = 1/16.

More offspring with no recessive phenotype generally strengthen the homozygous interpretation, but finite samples still require cautious wording. Say what the evidence supports and what remains possible.

blocks.text: Worked exampleA recessive offspring resolves the unknownA black fictional mouse, B_, is crossed with a brown bb mouse. One offspring is brown.The brown offspring is bb.The known tester supplied one b.The unknown black parent supplied the other b, so it carries b.Its black phenotype also requires B in the complete-dominance model.The unknown parent is Bb.

Use family information before calculatingAdditional parent or offspring information can resolve an unknown genotype. A dominant-phenotype individual with an aa parent must have received a from that parent, so it must be Aa. You do not need another test cross to establish that conclusion within the model.Start with the most informative constraints. Write the alleles that must be present, preserve unknowns where necessary, and only then calculate the next cross. Guessing an unresolved genotype can make every later arithmetic step misleading.
